reconcile.connective: JFB reads 10:23's "coming of the Son of man" as the imminent AD 70 judgment on Jerusalem, not the end of the world, and states outright that this reading runs parallel with Matthew 24:14's timetable.

discrepancy.connective: Albert Schweitzer took Matthew 10:23 as Jesus' own genuine expectation that the end would arrive within the Twelve's Israelite mission -- a timetable Matthew 24:14's worldwide-preaching requirement cannot honor.

skeptic.name: Albert Schweitzer
skeptic.work: The Quest of the Historical Jesus
skeptic.attribution: Albert Schweitzer (1875-1965), The Quest of the Historical Jesus (Von Reimarus zu Wrede, 1906; Eng. trans. 1910)

excerpts.excerpt_text: "The coming of the Son of man" has a fixed doctrinal sense, here referring immediately to the crisis of Israel's history as the visible kingdom of God, when Christ was to come and judge it … but only as being such a lively anticipation of His second coming for vengeance and deliverance. So understood, it is parallel with Mat 24:14 (on which see).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB explicitly identifies the 'coming of the Son of man' in 10:23 as the AD 70 judgment-coming (only an anticipation of the true Parousia, not the end of the world), and states outright that this reading is 'parallel with Mat 24:14' -- directly addressing why the two verses need not describe the same eschatological event on the same timetable, which is the crux of 'When will the end of the world come?'

pd_work.resource: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown, Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible (1871)
pd_work.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
pd_work.note: JFB treats Matthew 10:23 directly, reading its 'coming of the Son of man' as the AD 70 judgment on Jerusalem rather than the end of the world, and explicitly cross-references the verse as parallel with Matthew 24:14. (Haley's Alleged Discrepancies could not be confirmed to cover this specific passage, so this row-surfaced harmonizing commentator is used per the spec's fallback.)
